alloc.rule: base weights by regime — equity / metals / bonds / cash: Goldilocks 70/10/15/5, Reflation 65/15/5/15, Stagflation 35/30/10/25, Disinflation 55/10/30/5 — blended by the nowcast's regime probabilities (so the book never jumps on a label change); the gate moves ten points from equity to cash. Half the equity is the core (Nifty 50 and Next 50); half goes to three sleeves the regime favours that are also trending — never to an UNDERWEIGHT. Gold is the metal sleeve (silver joins when it trends). Long gilts in Disinflation and Goldilocks, short gilts otherwise, halved when gilts trend down. Cash is the residual.
alloc.how: each sleeve is measured on its long index in rupees since 2015 (the ETF is what you trade), labelled week by week with the same CPI × IIP regime path the rest of the page uses; the number is the average forward 13-week return in that regime and the share of weeks that paid. Windows overlap, so n counts weeks, not independent quarters. Trend is the ETF against its 40-week average and its 13-week return; the word needs the trend, and the regime's record may confirm or veto it. A map of what each regime has paid — not a forecast, not a backtest of the allocation.

attr.how: a move counts when it is ≥ 1.5σ (and ≥ 2%) on a liquid name; the market's part is the name's three-year Nifty β times the Nifty's day, the sector's part the sector's median move relative to the Nifty (capped at the move itself), the rest is the stock's own; STOCK-SPECIFIC when the own part is ≥ 60% of the move. The delivery read is NSE's deliverable-quantity figure against the name's own twenty-session average.

street.how: Yahoo's mean analyst target (names with ≥ 5 analysts) as an upside from today's price, against the engine's twelve-month expectation; the gap is engine minus Street in points of upside. The two disagree by construction more often than not: a consensus target lags the price, so the Street's biggest upsides sit on names that have fallen, while the engine's expectation leans on momentum, the regime and the company's numbers. The widest gaps can also be a stale target after a split or a demerger. The record freezes the twenty widest gaps each day and, sixty sessions on, asks whose implied path the price came closer to.
